clue.text: Highland castle, central part opening, we hear?

indicators.note: a phrase about listening, so the two words built here are said aloud rather than written

parts.note: the core of something is its central part; a door is an opening into a building

explanation.surface: A tourist describes a Scottish castle, perhaps its central archway, as heard on a guided tour.
explanation.walkthrough: In a non-rhotic British accent CORE DOOR, said quickly, sounds like the castle's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Cawdor Castle stands near Nairn in the Scottish Highlands, famous from Macbeth's title Thane of Cawdor.

clue.text: Where servers cut, machine with battery dead

parts.note: a car is a machine fitted with a battery
in informal British speech dead means very, as in 'dead easy'

explanation.surface: Some device has stopped working because its battery has died.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dead' looks like a description of the battery, but it is the slang intensifier, as in 'dead good'.
explanation.definitionFit: A carvery is a restaurant counter where staff slice roast joints for diners.

clue.text: See 20
Amount produced revealed change

parts.note: a secret that is out has been revealed
to turn is to change, as milk turns sour

explanation.surface: A production figure was disclosed and turned out to have shifted.
explanation.definitionFit: Outturn is the quantity of goods a factory or harvest yields in a given period.

clue.text: Caution shown when playing king, fearful scoundrel nicking it?

parts.note: yellow means cowardly or fearful

indicators.note: the scoundrel nicks, that is steals and holds, the king, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: a cad is a dishonourable man, a scoundrel
R, from Latin rex, is the abbreviation for king

explanation.surface: A cowardly rogue steals the king while a card game is in play, and someone urges caution.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Playing' and 'king' suggest a card game; the caution is a referee's in a sport.
explanation.definitionFit: In football a referee shows a yellow card as a formal warning, called a caution, to an offending player.

clue.text: Flower and rotten nut they leave on stage

parts.note: a flower is something that flows, a river: the Exe in Devon

indicators.note: something rotten has gone bad, so these letters are spoilt into a new order

explanation.surface: A bloom and a decayed nut are cleared away by the departing stagehands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flower' reads as a bloom but is a crossword river, here the Exe in south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: Exeunt is the Latin stage direction meaning several characters go off together.

clue.text: Old trainer in ring made of metal, iron

indicators.note: the answer is made out of these letters, rearranged

explanation.surface: An old circus trainer works inside a ring built of metal and iron bars.
explanation.walkthrough: The fodder is METAL IRON; 'made of' turns them into a new nine letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Circus big-cat handlers performed in the ring, an act now largely banned, hence old.

clue.text: Shrimpy shrimp went

parts.note: shrimpy means tiny, and wee is Scottish for small
a shrimp is a puny person, a weed

explanation.surface: A tiny prawn simply departed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Went' as a definition is a euphemism: to go is to urinate.
explanation.definitionFit: Childish slang for urinated; 'went' is the coy past tense of going to the toilet.

clue.text: Pay cut with last of cheques in post, frantic

parts.note: to atone is to pay for a wrong

indicators.note: the trimmed word and the letter sit inside the posting word

parts.note: to post a letter is to send it

indicators.note: a word that is cut loses its final letter here
the closing letter of the word cheques is taken

explanation.surface: Someone whose wages were slashed, with the final cheque still in the mail, is desperate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut' acts on 'with', leaving WIT; add S and put WITS inside SEND.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone at their wits' end is so worried and exasperated that they are frantic.

clue.text: Test of right and left, all characters on the far left

indicators.text: all characters on the far left
indicators.note: every word's leftmost character, its first letter, is taken

explanation.surface: An exam on telling right from left, with every letter pushed hard to the left margin.
explanation.walkthrough: The first letters of 'of right and left' are taken; 'Test' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An oral is a spoken examination, a test conducted by question and answer.

clue.text: See 12
Vale on borders of Cymru, reportedly?

indicators.note: something reported is passed on in speech, so the letters are taken as said aloud

parts.note: the outer letters, the borders, of the word Cymru are C and U

explanation.surface: A Welsh valley lies along the edges of Wales, so they say.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vale' looks like a valley, but it is Latin for farewell. Cymru is the Welsh name for Wales; its outer letters C U spoken give the parting phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Latin vale means goodbye, matching the casual parting phrase used when leaving someone.

clue.text: Square peg moved then to practise intuitive approach quickly, so to speak?

parts.note: nine is a square number, three times three
a tee is the peg a golfer sets the ball on

indicators.note: the letters are moved about into a new order

parts.note: to do something is to practise it, as in doing yoga
Zen Buddhism stresses intuition over reasoning

explanation.surface: A misfit is shifted to practise a gut-feel method in a hurry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Moved' rearranges THEN TO into NTOTHE. 'Square peg' tempts as a misfit; it splits into a number and a golf tee.
explanation.definitionFit: Talking nineteen to the dozen means chattering very rapidly, hence quickly in speech.

clue.text: Very old woman said to predict failure in honest spy

definitions.text: Very old woman said to predict

indicators.note: a failure in the spy's letters means they break down into a new order

explanation.surface: An elderly fortune-teller foresees an honest spy's downfall.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram of HONEST SPY is signalled by 'failure in'.
explanation.definitionFit: A pythoness was a priestess of Apollo at Delphi, an ancient prophetess who foretold the future.

clue.text: A beauty has boss and I overwhelmed by lust

indicators.note: being overwhelmed means engulfed, so these pieces sit inside the word for lust

parts.note: hunger is a strong desire, lust
MD, managing director, is a company boss

explanation.surface: A handsome person is the boss's, and the speaker is swept up in desire.
explanation.definitionFit: A humdinger is a remarkable or outstanding person or thing, a real beauty.

clue.text: In Potsdam, I design pots!

indicators.note: to pot is to put something inside a container, so these words hold the answer

explanation.surface: A potter in the German city of Potsdam announces their designs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pots' looks like the potter's wares but is a verb: the words hold the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Amid means in the middle of, among, as a preposition like in.

clue.text: Third note, then second note

parts.note: me, or mi, is the third note of the sol-fa scale
mo is short for moment, a second

explanation.surface: A musician names a third note and then a second note in a scale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second note' looks like a musical term but splits: 'second' gives MO, and 'note' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A memo is a brief written note, short for memorandum.

clue.text: Revealing garment, quick way to dress topless crime writer

indicators.note: the road wraps around the writer like clothing

parts.note: the M1 is a British motorway, a quick route north from London

indicators.note: the writer's name loses its top, its first letter

parts.note: Ian Rankin is a Scottish crime novelist, creator of Rebus

explanation.surface: Wrapping a shirtless crime novelist in skimpy clothing is the fastest way.
explanation.walkthrough: M1 (a motorway) becomes MI; Ian Rankin is the Scottish author of the Rebus novels.
explanation.definitionFit: A mankini is a skimpy one-piece male swimsuit that reveals almost everything.

clue.text: Travesty reversed in perfect game for children

indicators.note: one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: in mint condition means perfect

indicators.note: the word for a travesty is read backwards

parts.note: a farce is a travesty, an absurd mockery

explanation.surface: A mockery turned upside down inside a flawless game for kids.
explanation.definitionFit: Minecraft is a block-building video game hugely popular with young players.

clue.text: Fugitive better protected by witness after heading for Egypt

indicators.note: the witness piece follows the Egypt letter
the head of a word is its first letter
the better piece is shielded within the witness word

parts.note: to witness is to see
to cap is to better or outdo

explanation.surface: A runaway shields a gambler behind a witness as they set off for Egypt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Better' reads as a gambler or as 'superior' but is a verb: to cap or top.
explanation.definitionFit: An escapee is someone who has escaped, such as from prison, a fugitive.

clue.text: Social life oddly uplifting for life form on Venus?

indicators.note: in a down clue, lifting up means the letters read from bottom to top, backwards

parts.note: a social is a party

indicators.note: the odd-numbered letters of the word life are taken

explanation.surface: A cheerful social life lifts the spirits of a lifeform on the planet Venus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Venus' points at the planet, but it names the plant, the Venus flytrap.
explanation.definitionFit: The Venus flytrap is a carnivorous plant, a life form named after Venus.

clue.text: Picture puzzle endures, did you say, on mural, fancifully?

indicators.note: a question about what was said, so the word is taken as spoken

parts.note: something that wears well endures
a whimsical adjective: mural means of a wall, so fancifully wall-y

explanation.surface: A puzzle picture that lasts, you ask, painted fancifully on a wall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mural' as an adjective means of a wall; 'fancifully' signals the coined adjective wall-y, built on the same pattern.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a series of children's picture books in which readers hunt for a striped-jumpered figure in crowded scenes.

clue.text: After refurbishment, Chinese restaurant at first improves

indicators.note: a refurbished thing has been done up afresh, so the letters are rearranged
only the opening letter of the word is taken

explanation.surface: Once redecorated, a Chinese restaurant gets better.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After refurbishment' rearranges CHINESE plus R, the opening letter of 'restaurant'.
explanation.definitionFit: To enrich something is to improve its quality or value.

clue.text: Bony thing, angle on figure by the sound of it?

indicators.note: the pieces are taken as heard, not as spelt

parts.note: to cock a hat is to set it at an angle, and six is a figure; one beside the other

explanation.surface: Something bony is tilted on a numeral, it seems.
explanation.definitionFit: The coccyx is the tailbone, a small bone at the base of the spine.

clue.text: Candies and chocolates and others: source of all of those?

definitions.text: Candies and chocolates and others: source of all of those?

indicators.note: the source of each listed word is its starting letter

explanation.surface: A shopper asks where all sweets and chocolates come from.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is wordplay and definition at once: the first letters spell the bean that chocolate comes from.
explanation.definitionFit: Cacao beans are the raw seeds from which cocoa and all chocolate confectionery are made.

clue.text: Biscuit that's new behind unopened sponge cakes, filling hole

indicators.note: the trimmed cakes and letter fill the hole word

parts.note: a gap is a hole

indicators.note: the new letter comes after the cakes
the word loses its opening letter

parts.note: sponge fingers are small finger-shaped sponge cakes

explanation.surface: A biscuit is fresh, tucked behind some unwrapped sponges that plug a gap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sponge cakes' gives FINGERS, as in sponge fingers; 'unopened' drops its F.
explanation.definitionFit: A gingersnap is a crisp, ginger-flavoured biscuit.

clue.text: See 4
Sudden flood of arrivals ruins new hospital

indicators.note: making the word new gives a fresh arrangement of its letters

parts.note: H is the map abbreviation for hospital

explanation.surface: A sudden crowd of patients wrecks a newly built hospital.
explanation.definitionFit: An inrush is a sudden influx, a surge of people or water pouring in.

clue.text: Get back on with success

parts.note: re means on or about, as in a letter heading
a coup is a notable success

explanation.surface: Get on with things and you will find success again.
explanation.definitionFit: To recoup losses is to regain or recover them.
